content: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) have become significant global health challenges due to inadequate management of drug-susceptible TB and the transmission of drug-resistant strains. While MDR/RR-TB is treatable, it often requires complex treatment regimens that are longer in duration and involve medications with potentially severe toxicities. This has driven efforts to develop shorter, safer, and more effective treatment regimens. In 2016, based on observational studies conducted in Asia and Africa, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended a standardized 9-month treatment regimen for eligible patients. This regimen included an injectable agent and was shorter than the standard 18–20 months of care. By 2018, modifications were made to this regimen, replacing kanamycin with amikacin due to evidence of better outcomes and reduced toxicity. However, the long-term toxic effects of injectable agents prompted further advancements, leading to the development of shorter, all-oral regimens. In 2019, WHO reviewed data from South Africa on a 9-month all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline. This regimen was subsequently recommended and included a combination of bedaquiline, levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin), ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (600 mg daily). The Nix-TB study, conducted by the Global TB Alliance, evaluated a novel 6-month regimen (BPaL) consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid. This regimen was designed for patients with MDR/RR-TB and additional resistance to fluoroquinolones. The study demonstrated promising outcomes, but limitations in study design and the small number of participants raised concerns about the generalizability of the findings. As a result, WHO recommended the BPaL regimen for use under operational research conditions in 2020. The ZeNix trial, completed in 2021, compared two variations of the BPaL regimen: one with a lower dose of linezolid (600 mg daily for 26 weeks) and another with the original higher dose (1200 mg daily for 26 weeks). The trial found that the lower-dose regimen reduced adverse events, such as peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression, without compromising treatment success. However, the certainty of the evidence was rated very low due to the small sample size and potential confounding factors. The WHO panel judged that the benefits of the lower-dose linezolid regimen were moderate, with trivial undesirable effects compared to the higher-dose regimen. The reduced pill burden and fewer adverse events were valued by patients and healthcare providers. Additionally, the lower-dose regimen was associated with moderate cost savings due to reduced drug costs and fewer adverse event-related expenses. The panel concluded that the balance of health effects probably favors the lower-dose linezolid regimen (600 mg daily for 26 weeks) as part of the BPaL treatment for MDR/RR-TB and pre-XDR-TB. This regimen is likely acceptable to stakeholders and feasible to implement, provided that drug safety monitoring and susceptibility testing are in place. However, further research is needed to strengthen the evidence base and address uncertainties.
